title: Restore IP Addresses
statement:
A dotted-decimal IPv4 address was written down and then every dot was lost, leaving only the digit string `s`. Recover all the addresses that could have produced `s`.

An IPv4 address is four decimal parts separated by dots, each part holding a number from 0 to 255 written without leading zeros, except that the number zero is written as the single digit `0`. Putting the four parts together in order must reproduce `s` exactly, so no digit may be dropped, reordered, or shared between two parts.

Return every valid address in ascending lexicographic order, and return an empty array when `s` cannot be split into four valid parts.

Examples: `s = "10112"` yields `["1.0.1.12", "1.0.11.2", "10.1.1.2"]`, and `s = "010010"` yields `["0.10.0.10", "0.100.1.0"]`.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 12`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Three dots are all the structure there is: four parts, each between one and three digits long, use every digit exactly once.
Prune while cutting. A part with a leading zero can only be the single digit `0`, and a part above 255 is dead, along with every longer part cut at the same spot.
Do not forget the leftover length rule: after three parts are placed, the rest is the fourth part, and its length has to be between one and three before you recurse any further.

editorial.approach: The brute force fixes the three dot positions with three nested loops over part lengths 1, 2 and 3, derives the length of the last part from what remains, validates all four parts, and sorts whatever it collected. The number of triples is at most C(n-1, 3), which is 165 for `n = 12`. The optimal version is a depth-first search with four levels that prunes at the point of choice: a part that is longer than one digit and starts with `0` kills the branch, a part whose value exceeds 255 kills the branch, and a part length that would leave fewer than one or more than three digits per remaining part is skipped before recursing. Both versions sort the answers, because the depth-first order (short first parts before long ones) is not lexicographic order on the finished addresses.
editorial.why_optimal: Four parts of at most three digits give a search tree with at most 3^4 = 81 leaves, and the pruning cuts whole subtrees at the root, so the search does a constant amount of work regardless of how long `s` is; the same argument makes the nested loops `O(n³)` with `n <= 12`, at most 165 triples. The unavoidable cost is formatting and sorting the answers, which both versions share, so the two implementations differ by a small constant factor here and the pruning only becomes decisive when narrower bounds stop the loops from finishing early.
editorial.pitfalls: Leading zeros are the classic bug: `"01"` is not a legal part, so `"010010"` must not produce `"01.0.0.10"`, and the check has to be done on the text of the part rather than on its numeric value, because `int("010")` is happily 10. Values above 255 have to be rejected, and the rejection must break out of the length loop rather than continue, since a longer part cut from the same position is only larger. The last part has no choice about its length, so a search that only ever places four parts of length 1 to 3 will silently drop solutions such as `"1.0.11.2"`, and a search that does not check `start == n` will emit addresses built from a prefix of `s`. Finally, `len(s) < 4` or `len(s) > 12` can never be split, so the early return has to be there.

solutions.title: Brute Force
solutions.complexity: Time: O(n³) (at most 165 cut triples at n = 12) | Space: O(1) extra

solutions.title: Optimal
solutions.complexity: Time: O(1) (at most 81 pruned placements) | Space: O(1) extra
